title: Schopenhauer
keyWorks: The World as Will and Representation (1819)
Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)
summary: Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher who believed that at the root of everything lies a blind, insatiable “will” — an endless striving that is never finally satisfied. Hence his famous pessimism. But he also found ways out: compassion, art and quiet contemplation, in which the will falls silent for a while.
onEmotions: For Schopenhauer, feelings are how the will feels from the inside: desire, lack, fear of loss, brief relief. He considered suffering not a mistake or a personal failure but the basic fabric of life — so there is nothing shameful in it. Relief comes not from fulfilling every desire (that is impossible) but from moments when we stop only wanting and begin to look: in music, in nature, in art. And the understanding that others suffer just as we do gives rise to compassion — for Schopenhauer, the basis of all morality.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a very understandable feeling, and it is not your fault. Schopenhauer described the human being as a manifestation of the “will” — a blind striving that constantly reaches forward into the future and is always afraid of something. From this point of view, anxiety is not a malfunction but the voice of the will itself, which doesn't know how to settle down. Schopenhauer advised not arguing with this restless striving head-on but stepping out of it from time to time. He called this “aesthetic contemplation”: when you truly look at a cloud or a tree, or listen to music, for a moment you stop being the one who wants and fears and become simply the one who sees. Anxiety doesn't vanish for good, but it gets a respite — and you discover that there is more in you than anxiety.
anxiety.practice: Choose one object near you — a cup, a leaf, a patch of sky — and for a minute simply look at it, wanting nothing from it. Notice what happens to your anxiety in that minute.

fear.text: Fear is one of the most ancient feelings, and it is natural to feel it. Schopenhauer believed that everything alive is pervaded by the “will to live” — an unconscious striving to exist and preserve oneself. Fear, from this point of view, is its most direct expression: the will protects itself before we've even had time to think. So there's no sense in scolding yourself for being afraid — fear is older than your character and your decisions. Schopenhauer distinguished the will from “representation” — our ability to see the world as a picture. When you can describe your fear in words, as if examining it from the outside, you partly cross over from will into representation. The fear remains, but it stops being your whole world: someone appears who is looking at it.
fear.practice: Describe your fear in three sentences as if you were telling about it from the outside: where it sits in your body, what it's like, what it wants.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and Schopenhauer would be the last person to demand cheerfulness from you. He believed life by its very structure is closer to lack than to fullness: the satisfaction of desires is brief, while desire itself is long. So sadness is not a sign that something is wrong with you but rather a sober perception of how the world is made. There is an unexpected comfort in this: you are not alone in your sorrow; all living beings share it. From this understanding Schopenhauer derived “compassion” — a feeling of shared fate with all who suffer. He also especially valued music: in his view, it expresses the will itself directly, without words, which is why a sad melody can console more deeply than any advice.
sadness.practice: Put on music that sounds the way your sadness feels, and simply listen, without trying to “cheer yourself up.” What did you hear in it about yourself?

grief.text: Grief after a loss is one of the hardest experiences, and it needs time. Schopenhauer wrote a great deal about transience: everything that comes into being passes away, and this is true of everything we love. He didn't prettify this truth. But his philosophy holds another thought as well: behind individual beings stands a single will, one and the same essence manifesting in each of us. From this point of view, your bond with the one you lost was not an illusion: in love you recognized yourself in the other. Schopenhauer considered such recognition the basis of compassion and the most genuine thing in a human being. Grief is the price of that recognition, and the fact that it hurts speaks of the depth of the bond, not of weakness.
grief.practice: Write down one trait of the person or thing you lost that you also recognize in yourself. Let that connection simply be.

loneliness.text: Loneliness can be very painful, and that pain deserves attention. Schopenhauer — himself a rather lonely man — looked at loneliness in two ways. He noticed that what often draws us to company is not love but boredom and inner emptiness. Hence his parable of the porcupines: in the cold they huddle together, but prick one another with their quills and move apart, until they find a “moderate distance.” On the other hand, he valued solitude as a time when a person can be themselves, without masks. From this point of view, loneliness is not a sentence but a search for your own distance: not too far from the warmth, not too close to the quills. And time alone can be not only endured but filled — with a book, music, reflection.
loneliness.practice: Think: what distance from other people would be “moderate” for you right now — a little closer or a little further than now? Write down one small step in that direction.

quote.text: A man can be himself only so long as he is alone.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)

anger.text: Anger is a strong feeling, and it often tells you that something matters to you. Schopenhauer would explain it as the will colliding with an obstacle: you want something, the world resists, and the will boils over. He also noted that all beings are different manifestations of one and the same will, constantly colliding with one another like hungry creatures in a crowded space. From this point of view, the person you're angry with is also gripped by their own will and suffers from it. Schopenhauer didn't call for suppressing anger, but he pointed to a way out through “compassion”: seeing in the other the same tormented being. This doesn't cancel your right to boundaries, but it can loosen anger's grip and give you back your clarity.
anger.practice: Name what exactly your will wanted in the moment of anger and what stood in its way. Then ask: what did the other person want, and what were they afraid of?

shame.text: Shame is a very painful feeling, and you don't have to be ashamed of it. Schopenhauer examined closely how much we depend on the opinion of others. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he distinguished what a person is, what a person has, and how a person appears in the eyes of others — and held that we value the last far too highly. In his view, most of our woundedness is tied precisely to others' opinion, which lives only in other people's heads. From this point of view, shame often says more about the power of other people's gaze than about your real worth. Schopenhauer advised shifting the weight from “how I seem” to “what I am”: your inner world, your abilities, your peace of mind.
shame.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “how I seem to others” and “what I am.” Where does the thing you're ashamed of right now belong?

guilt.text: Guilt can be heavy, and it's worth meeting it gently. Schopenhauer believed our actions flow from our character, and our character from a will we did not choose. It sounds like an excuse, but he drew a different conclusion: conscience shows us not only a single deed but who we are. From this point of view, guilt is knowledge about yourself, not a verdict. Even more important is his idea of “compassion”: he considered the ability to feel another's pain as your own the basis of morality. If it hurts you that you harmed someone, then compassion is alive in you. And you can turn that same compassion toward yourself: you too are a living being, gripped by the will and capable of making mistakes.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: what does this guilt say about what matters to you? Write down one small action through which you can express that.

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but very human feeling, and there's no shame in feeling it. Schopenhauer saw it as one of the natural expressions of the will: we measure our well-being not in itself but by comparing it with others'. He noticed that our contentment depends on the ratio between what we want and what we have: as soon as we see in someone else what we lack, the lack suddenly sharpens. From this point of view, envy is not so much about the other person as about an emptiness in your own desire that has suddenly been lit up. Schopenhauer advised turning your gaze to what you already have, and remembering: someone else's life, seen from outside, looks happier than it is from within. Behind every façade is the same unquenched will.
envy.practice: Write down what exactly you wanted when you felt envy. Is the desire about the thing itself, or about the feeling you imagine it gives?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be frightening: it seems that nothing touches you. Schopenhauer described two states of the will: when it wants and doesn't have, that is suffering; when it has obtained, boredom and emptiness set in, because the desire has vanished and a new one hasn't come yet. From this point of view, emptiness is not a sign that you're “broken” but a natural pause in the will's work. But Schopenhauer also saw an opportunity in such pauses. When desire quiets down, room opens up for “disinterested” contemplation — looking at the world while demanding nothing of it. That is how we look at art and at nature. There's no need to rush to fill the emptiness with a new chase; sometimes it's enough to let your eyes simply rest on something beautiful.
emptiness.practice: Find one thing today you can look at for the sake of looking — a painting, the light from a window, a pattern. Stay with it for a minute with no purpose at all.

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal state when your familiar picture of the world stops working. Schopenhauer opened his main book with the words that the world is our “representation”: everything we know, we know through our own way of seeing — through time, space and causality. From this point of view, confusion is the moment when you notice that your representation doesn't match what's happening. It's unpleasant, but honest. Schopenhauer also held that behind representation stands the will — what we truly want, often without realizing it. So sometimes confusion clears up not through new reasoning but through a question: what is it that wants something in me, deeper than my thoughts? The answer may not come at once — and that's all right too.
confusion.practice: Write two sentences: “I think I should…” and “Somewhere deeper, I want…” See where they diverge.

quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 1 (1819)

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not laziness or weakness but an honest signal that you've reached the limit of your strength. Schopenhauer described life as ceaseless striving: having reached one goal, the will immediately sets the next, and so on without end. From this point of view, burnout is what happens when for years we live only in “want and achieve” mode, never stepping off the wheel. Schopenhauer compared this state to the wheel of Ixion from Greek myth, which turns without stopping — and wrote that it can be halted for a while by moments of contemplation, when we aren't trying to achieve anything. Rest, in this sense, is not a reward for accomplishments but a right to a respite from the will, one everyone needs.
fatigue.practice: Notice how many times today you thought “I have to.” Choose one minute in which you don't have to do anything, and simply breathe.

boredom.text: Boredom seems like a trivial feeling, but Schopenhauer took it seriously. He believed life swings between two poles: when we lack something, we suffer; when we have everything, boredom arrives. Boredom, in his view, is the sensation of the emptiness of existence itself, when the will has nothing to cling to. It sounds bleak, but there's relief in it: boredom is not your personal failure but part of a pendulum all humans share. The best remedy for it, Schopenhauer thought, was not new entertainments but “inner wealth”: interest in thoughts, books, art, observation. A person with a rich inner world, he wrote, depends less on the outer one. Boredom can become an invitation to make yourself a little more at home in that world.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: what would interest me if no one would ever know about it and it brought me nothing? Write down the first thing that comes to mind.

quote.text: Life swings like a pendulum backwards and forwards between pain and boredom.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 57 (1819)

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful feeling, and you can simply give yourself over to it. Schopenhauer, the famous pessimist, considered the satisfaction of desires brief, but he singled out a special kind of joy — the kind that comes in art and contemplation. When you are captured by music, a landscape or the beauty of a moment, you are, in his view, freed for a while from “serving the will”: you don't want, you don't fear, you simply are. He called this the state of the “pure subject of knowing” — the one who only sees. From this point of view, the deepest joy is not the one that comes from acquiring something but the one in which you forget yourself. It doesn't need to be held onto or justified. You can simply notice it — and know that you have the capacity for such joy.
joy.practice: Recall the moment today when you “forgot yourself” for a second. What was before your eyes or sounding around you?

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most precious feelings. Schopenhauer wrote about love in two ways. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love” he explained falling in love soberly, even harshly, as a ruse of the “will to live,” which strives to continue the species. But he rated another kind of love very highly — love in which you feel another's pain and joy as your own. In his view, in such moments the boundary between “I” and “you” fades, and you recognize in the other the very same essence as in yourself. From this point of view, tenderness is neither weakness nor illusion but a moment of insight: you see that the other is not a stranger to you. That, for Schopenhauer, lies at the root of all true kindness.
love.practice: Recall the last time you felt someone else's joy or pain almost as your own. What did you learn then about yourself and about the other?

quote.text: All true and pure love is compassion.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 66 (1819)

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and Schopenhauer helps us understand why it is so precious and so rare. He noticed that we take good things for granted, while we feel lack acutely. Health, peace, loved ones are almost invisible while we have them. In his view, happiness is “negative”: it consists above all in the absence of pain, and so it easily slips past our attention. From this point of view, gratitude is the ability to notice such a quiet good: that nothing hurts right now, that someone is near, that there's warm light in the window. Schopenhauer advised imagining from time to time what it would be like to lose what we have — not to frighten ourselves, but to see the value of what is already ours.
gratitude.practice: Name three “quiet” goods you have right now that you usually don't notice. Stay with each for a couple of seconds.

quote.text: We seldom think of what we have but always of what we lack.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life (1851)

hope.text: Hope sustains us in hard times, and it is natural to hold on to it. Schopenhauer was wary of hope: he saw that the will constantly promises itself happiness “out there, ahead,” and that this promise is rarely fulfilled the way we imagine. But his thought can be read not as a ban on hope but as advice to aim it more wisely. From this point of view, hope for complete and final happiness makes us vulnerable, while hope for good moments — music, a meeting, kindness, a quiet evening — is entirely realistic. Schopenhauer advised expecting less perfection from life and noticing more of what is possible. Such modest hope doesn't disappoint; it sustains.
hope.practice: Put your hope for the coming week into its smallest, most concrete form. What exactly would you like to happen?

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, sad longing for the past, and there is nothing wrong with it. Schopenhauer gave it an interesting explanation. He noticed that in memory the past seems brighter than it really was: the images remain, but the will disappears — the anxieties, desires and worries that tormented us at the time. We remember the past the way one looks at a painting — contemplatively. From this point of view, nostalgia is partly an “aesthetic” feeling: we long not only for time gone by but also for the freedom from desire that looking from the outside gives us. Which means a similar clarity is available in the present too — if you look at today as a future painting.
nostalgia.practice: Look at today the way you'll remember it ten years from now. Which one detail would you want to keep from it?

craving.text: A craving is a sharp “I want it right now,” and the fact that it's so strong says nothing bad about you. Schopenhauer would describe it as the “will” in its purest form: a blind striving older than our thoughts and stronger than our decisions. His main observation about the will: satisfaction quenches desire only briefly, and then it returns, often stronger. That's why a craving promises so convincingly that “now it'll feel good” — and so rarely keeps its promise. From this point of view, the craving is not your voice but the voice of the will sounding through you. You can listen to it like the weather: it rises, peaks and subsides. Schopenhauer would advise not arguing with it head-on but, for a minute, moving from “wanting” into observing — looking at it as a phenomenon of the world.
craving.practice: Describe your craving as if you were a researcher: where it is in your body, how strong it is from 1 to 10. After five minutes, note its strength again.

quote.text: Wealth is like sea-water; the more we drink, the thirstier we become; and the same is true of fame.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Ch. 3 (1851)

addiction.text: Addiction is a heavy, long-standing circle, and the fact that it's hard to get out of is not a moral failure or a weakness of character. Schopenhauer would explain this by the very nature of the “will”: it is insatiable, and once it has found a shortcut to relief, it will call you back there again and again. In his essay “On the Freedom of the Will” (1839) he argued that actions follow from character and “motives.” But he also stressed that motives act through knowledge — through what we see and how we see it. When understanding changes, what acts on us changes too. He also spoke of “acquired character” — a calm, honest knowledge of your own strengths and weaknesses, without self-deception and without self-flagellation. From this point of view, the way out begins not with reproaching yourself but with a clear look: what exactly does this circle give me, and what am I really missing?
addiction.practice: Finish the sentence: “When I reach for this, what I'm really missing is…” If you like, you can talk about it with someone who has walked a similar path — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after a heavy night can be agonizing: your body aches, and on top of that come anxiety, shame and gaps in memory. All of this is understandable, and you don't need to pile more on yourself. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer wrote that most of our well-being depends on health, and right now your body is simply making itself felt. And about shame he has a sober observation: we vastly exaggerate the importance of what others think of us — other people's opinions occupy them far less than it seems to us in the night-time replay of memory. From this point of view, the morning dread is largely the voice of the will, frightened for its place among people. Schopenhauer would suggest not deciding your fate or passing sentence on yourself today, but taking care of your body and letting the day pass.
hangover.practice: Do one simple thing for your body: drink a glass of water, open a window. Then name one fact about last night that you know for certain, separate from your fears about it.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, and you can enjoy it. Schopenhauer, for all his pessimism, especially prized cheerfulness: in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he calls it the “ready cash” of happiness — not a promise, but something you have right now. So, he wrote, we should open the door to it whenever it comes, without asking whether it has good reason to be there. At the same time he was honest: such a high is fleeting by nature, like any fulfilment of desire. From this point of view, the wisdom here lies not in holding on to euphoria but in living it without building your whole life's plans on it. Allow yourself to enjoy the light of this moment, and don't demand that it last forever.
euphoria.practice: Write one sentence about what seems beautiful or possible to you right now. Reread it tomorrow with a calm eye — what in it will still be yours?

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be very hard, as if the floor had been pulled out from under you. It's an understandable reaction, not proof that something is wrong with you. Schopenhauer described these swings very precisely. In The World as Will and Representation (§ 57) he noted that all excessive jubilation rests on the illusion that final satisfaction has been found — and when the illusion dissolves, a fall comes that matches the rise in strength. From this point of view, your “comedown” is not a punishment but the second half of the same wave. Schopenhauer saw real relief in understanding this mechanism: what you feel now is not a new truth about life but the swing of a pendulum, which will also pass. His advice is to keep an even keel: don't try to regain the height immediately, but let yourself come down onto solid ground.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “This is a comedown, not a verdict.” Then do one slow, everyday thing — make tea, make the bed — and notice how it feels.

panic.text: Panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart pounds, your breath falters, it seems something terrible is about to happen. This is genuinely hard for you, and that needs to be acknowledged. Schopenhauer saw the body as “the will made visible”: the heart, the breath, the tension of the muscles are the will to live sounding the alarm. From this point of view, panic is not your weakness but an ancient force of self-preservation that has gone off too loudly. Such a wave usually rises, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Schopenhauer also offers a way out from under the will's power: “pure contemplation,” when you stop wanting and simply look at the things around you. Even at the peak, you can shift a little in that direction — from the inner storm to the simple objects of the world.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and make your out-breath longer than your in-breath. Name aloud five objects you can see, and the colour of each.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what's the point of it all,” thoughts of finitude — is a very heavy experience, and you are not alone in it. Schopenhauer wrote that it is precisely the knowledge of death and suffering that most strongly drives people to philosophy; he called this the “metaphysical need” — the need to understand what it all means. From this point of view, your dread is not a malfunction but one of the deepest human questions, one that many before you have asked themselves. Schopenhauer offered no comforting illusions, but from this shared fragility he drew something important: since everyone faces the same thing, the most fitting way to treat one another is with compassion. In one of his late texts he even suggested seeing in everyone a “fellow sufferer.” This dread can become the place where tenderness toward yourself and others is born.
dread.practice: Think of one person who most likely also once asked themselves “what's the point of it all.” Silently wish them well — and yourself too.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you're not where you should be is very familiar and very draining. Schopenhauer described its roots almost two hundred years ago. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he distinguished what a person “is,” what they “have,” and how they “appear” in the eyes of others — and held that we vastly overrate the last. We see other people's shop windows, but our own life from the inside, with all its humdrum days. From this point of view, the comparison is unfair from the start. Besides, Schopenhauer reminded us that the only form in which life is given to us at all is the present; past and future exist only in thought. “Somewhere out there” is a representation, while “here” is the only place you can truly be.
fomo.practice: Name three things in your “here and now” that don't appear in any shop window: a sound, a smell, a sensation.

sleepless.text: Sleeplessness and thoughts at three in the morning can be especially agonizing: everything seems huge and hopeless. A great many people know this. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer called morning the “youth of the day” — a time of freshness and clarity — and evening its “old age.” From this point of view, night-time thoughts are no truer than daytime ones; it's just that the will, tired and left alone with itself, paints everything black. Schopenhauer would suggest making no decisions at night and not trying to think the thought through to the end. You can politely set it aside until morning and, in the dark, return to contemplation — to the sound of your breathing, the stillness of the room, to what simply is.
sleepless.practice: Write the troubling thought down in one line and add: “I'll come back to this in the morning.” Then count ten slow out-breaths.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds very deeply: what collapses is not only a relationship but your trust in your own judgment. Your pain is justified. Schopenhauer believed a person's character is inborn and fundamentally unchanging: people reveal who they are gradually, and no one can see another's character in full in advance. From this point of view, you weren't “stupid” to trust — you simply couldn't know what only the act revealed. Schopenhauer was sober in his conclusions too: he advised not throwing away bitter experience but keeping it as knowledge about the person. But sobriety doesn't require bitterness. He also taught that we are all manifestations of one blind will, and this lets you understand without excusing. You can protect yourself and still not turn into the one who hurt you.
betrayal.practice: Write two sentences: “What I now know about this person” and “What good I still know about myself.”

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a burning feeling, and there's no shame in feeling it: it shows how much the person means to you. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love,” Schopenhauer explained the force of amorous passions by the fact that what acts through us is not only personal desire but the “will to live” itself — ancient, stubborn, never asking our opinion. From this point of view, jealousy is the voice of that will, afraid of losing. That's why it's so strong and listens so poorly to reason. Understanding this helps you step a little to the side: you are not only your jealousy; you are also the one who sees it. From this observer's position it's easier to choose what to say and do, and what simply to live through inwardly without destroying yourself or the relationship.
jealousy.practice: Tell yourself: “What's speaking in me right now is the fear of losing.” Write down, in one word, what exactly you're afraid of losing.

resentment.text: A long-held grudge is a heavy load you carry with you for years, and behind it there is almost always real pain. Schopenhauer helps you look at it from a new angle. He believed that people's actions follow from their character, and character hardly changes. It sounds bleak, but a liberating conclusion follows: you can stop waiting for the person who hurt you to one day become someone else and put everything right. From this point of view, a grudge is often held in place by this very waiting. Schopenhauer went further: he saw in all beings manifestations of one and the same blind will, which suffers and causes suffering. This understanding doesn't cancel the fact that you were in the right, but it can loosen the grip: the one who hurt you was also gripped by a force they barely understood.
resentment.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm still waiting for this person to…” Then ask yourself: what of what I'm waiting for from them could I give myself?

heartbreak.text: A breakup and a broken heart can feel like a disproportionate, almost cosmic pain. Schopenhauer gave this a remarkable explanation. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love” he wrote that in amorous passion it is not only the individual who acts but the “will to live” of the whole species; that's why the sufferings of love are so immense — in them, he said, something greater than the individual groans. From this point of view, the force of your pain is not a sign of weakness or “oversensitivity”: you have run into one of the most powerful forces of nature. Schopenhauer would suggest treating yourself with the same compassion he considered the basis of morality, and giving yourself respites in contemplation — in music, nature, books, where the will falls silent at least for a while.
heartbreak.practice: Put on one piece of music that feels close to you and listen to it to the end, doing nothing else. Just let it sound together with your sadness.

impostor.text: The feeling that you're about to be exposed is very widespread, and it especially often visits conscientious people. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer distinguished three things: what a person “is,” what they “have,” and how they “appear” in others' eyes. He held that people spend an inordinate amount of energy on the third — on how they look in others' opinion — and that this is one of the chief sources of unease. From this point of view, impostor syndrome is a fear for your “appearance,” not for what you “are.” Schopenhauer advised shifting the weight onto what stays with you whatever the judgments: your knowledge, your qualities, your work. Judgments change, but what you've done already exists.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you can really do or have done — facts, not judgments. Reread them when “they'll find me out” washes over you again.

self_hatred.text: Self-hatred and a harsh inner critic cause enormous pain, and you don't deserve this verdict. Schopenhauer believed a person's basic character is not chosen: we receive it just as we receive the colour of our eyes. From this point of view, the inner critic demands the impossible of you — to be someone else entirely. Schopenhauer offered something different: “acquired character,” that is, a calm, clear knowledge of your strengths and weaknesses, with which a person stops waging war on themselves and finds their place. And he considered the chief virtue to be “compassion” — the ability to see in another the same suffering will as in oneself. If every living being deserves compassion, there's no reason to exclude yourself from that circle.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine your inner critic speaking to a stranger. What would you say in that person's defence, out of compassion? Say it to yourself.

helplessness.text: Helplessness, the feeling that you can't change anything, is a very heavy state, and it is not your fault. Schopenhauer wrote a great deal about necessity: much in life — circumstances, character, the course of events — does not bend to our wishes. But in understanding this he saw not despair but a kind of consolation: in The World as Will and Representation he noted that nothing reconciles us to an unavoidable misfortune so much as a clear grasp of its necessity — that it could not have been otherwise. From this point of view, it's worth separating what is beyond your power from the tiny bit that is within it. And one more thing: powerlessness is a shared human condition. Schopenhauer suggested seeing others as “fellow sufferers,” which means you aren't alone in this either.
helplessness.practice: Draw two circles: “beyond my power” and “a little within my power.” In the second, write one very small action for today.

procrastination.text: The “I can't get started” state is exhausting, and it isn't laziness. Schopenhauer would explain it through the nature of the “will”: it is constantly torn between many desires and fears, and when there are too many of them, movement gets stuck. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he makes a simple observation: all limitation makes for happiness. The narrower the circle of our concerns and possibilities, the less we are troubled and the calmer the will. From this point of view, procrastination often grows out of too wide a horizon: the task is seen whole, with all its consequences and judgments. Schopenhauer's advice is to narrow your field of vision to a single step, without asking whether it will lead to success. It's easier for the will to move when what's before it is not a mountain but one stair.
procrastination.practice: Identify the smallest first step of your task — one that takes two minutes. Do only that, and give yourself permission to stop there.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — a move, emigration, the loss of familiar ground — is a very hard experience, and it needs time. Schopenhauer knew this firsthand: as a child he left his native Danzig with his family, lived for a long time in different cities and countries, and only settled in Frankfurt in his mature years. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he insisted that what matters most for a person is what they “are” — their inner qualities — not what they “have” or where they happen to be. From this point of view, you have carried the most valuable things with you: your mind, your abilities, your memory, your capacity to love. This doesn't cancel your longing for the place. But the ground beneath your feet need not be only external: part of it you carry inside.
uprooted.practice: Write down three things you brought with you not in a suitcase but within yourself: a skill, a habit, a memory.

overload.text: Overload, the endless feed, information noise — all of this really is tiring, and you don't have to keep up with everything. Schopenhauer foresaw this problem long before the internet. In his essays “On Reading and Books” and “On Thinking for Oneself” he warned that whoever constantly absorbs other people's thoughts gradually forgets how to think for themselves — the head becomes a playground for other people's thoughts. From this point of view, overload is not only fatigue but also a loss of your own voice. Schopenhauer valued silence and limitation: he believed our own thoughts come when room is left for them. A gentle response to overload is not willpower but a pause in which you let nothing in and allow yourself to hear what you are thinking.
overload.practice: Put your phone aside for two minutes. Write down one thought that came to you on its own, not from the feed.

quote.text: When we read, another person thinks for us.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: Parerga and Paralipomena, “On Reading and Books” (1851)

unreality.text: The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be very frightening, and it can be hard to talk about. Philosophers have long known something similar. Schopenhauer opened his main book with the words “the world is my representation”: we know the world only through how it appears to our consciousness. In § 5 he even admitted that the boundary between dreaming and waking is not as obvious as it seems. But he also has an important addition: there is one thing we know not only as a picture but from the inside — our own body. We feel it directly, as “will” — tension, warmth, movement. From this point of view, even when the world seems far away, the body remains the point where you are connected to reality from within.
unreality.practice: Clench and unclench your hands, feel their warmth. Tell yourself: “This is my body, and I feel it from the inside.”

quote.text: Life and dreams are leaves of one and the same book.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 5 (1819)

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience. Schopenhauer described it in detail under the name of “the sublime.” When we see a storm, mountains, a starry sky, we feel tiny before the forces of nature. But at the same time, he wrote, something else awakens in us: the “pure subject of knowing,” which calmly contemplates all this grandeur and is not afraid. Fear for oneself recedes, and we simply look. From this point of view, awe is one of those rare moments when the will in you falls silent and you become pure seeing. Schopenhauer considered such moments the best that life offers: in them, suffering and desire let go for a while. You don't need to do anything with it — just stay in it.
awe.practice: Linger for one more minute with whatever stirred your awe. Notice that in this moment you need nothing.

relief.text: Relief is a warm, quiet feeling, and it's worth savouring. Schopenhauer gave it special significance. He believed we feel suffering directly and sharply, while well-being is felt only as the absence of suffering. It sounds pessimistic, but a lovely conclusion follows: relief is the moment when we actually notice our happiness. Usually health, peace and safety are as invisible as air; only when the weight lifts do we feel how much we have. From this point of view, relief is a rare chance to see the value of the ordinary. Schopenhauer rated freedom from pain above the pursuit of pleasures, and that is exactly what you're experiencing now. Allow yourself simply to breathe out.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath and name one ordinary thing that, now, after the relief, you value more than you did yesterday.

calm.text: Calm and peace are a precious state, one that is good simply to rest in. Schopenhauer described it in his theory of contemplation. Usually, he wrote, we live under the sway of the “will” and spin like Ixion on his wheel in the Greek myth — with no respite from desires and fears. But there are moments when we look at the world without self-interest: at a sunset, at water, at the face of a sleeping child. Then, in his words, Ixion's wheel stands still, and a sabbath arrives, a respite from the penal servitude of willing. From this point of view, your calm is neither emptiness nor laziness but one of the best states available to a human being. Schopenhauer would not urge you to use it or prolong it by effort — only to notice it and cherish it.
calm.practice: Notice where in your body this calm is felt. Stay with that sensation for a minute, adding nothing.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful, living state, and it's good to receive it with gratitude. Schopenhauer believed the best thoughts and images come when we are freed for a while from personal concerns and begin to look at things “objectively” — without asking what they give us personally. He called this ability the essence of genius, but saw its seeds in everyone. In the essay “On Thinking for Oneself” he noted that your own thoughts cannot be summoned on command: they come by themselves when room is left for them. From this point of view, inspiration is your pure view of the world, freed from the bustle. Schopenhauer would advise you not to let it slip: write it down while it's here, and don't measure it by usefulness or by others' judgments.
inspiration.practice: Right now, write down whatever has come to you, in any form — words, a sketch, a list — without editing.

schadenfreude.text: Noticing schadenfreude in yourself is unpleasant, but almost everyone knows this feeling. Schopenhauer was strict about it: in On the Basis of Morality he saw joy at another's misfortune as the direct opposite of compassion. But his own philosophy explains where it comes from. Each of us, for Schopenhauer, carries an insatiable will and a constant lack. From this point of view: when your own burden is heavy, someone else's failure makes it lighter for a moment — “I'm not the only one.” Schadenfreude then speaks above all of your own pain. And then Schopenhauer suggests an important step: to see that the one who stumbled suffers from the very same will as you. The very ability to notice schadenfreude in yourself is already the beginning of compassion, not a reason to punish yourself.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: which pain of my own quieted for a second at someone else's failure? Name it in a word or two.

contempt.text: Contempt can be an understandable response to someone else's foolishness, cruelty or baseness. Schopenhauer knew this feeling himself: he made no secret of his contempt for fashionable philosophers and for “the crowd.” But in Parerga and Paralipomena he proposed a remedy that can soften even it. People, he wrote, should address one another as “fellow sufferers.” Such an address reminds us that each person carries the same blind will — desire, lack, fear — and that their weaknesses grew from the same soil as ours. From this point of view, contempt divides people into “higher” and “lower,” while compassion sees a shared plight. This doesn't cancel your judgment of the action. But it lets you avoid carrying a coldness that chills you yourself first of all.
contempt.practice: Try silently calling this person a “fellow sufferer.” What burden of their own can you imagine?

disgust.text: Disgust is a very bodily feeling: you want to turn away, draw back, wall yourself off. Schopenhauer spoke of it in his theory of art. The beautiful, in his view, allows us to stop wanting for a while and simply contemplate. The disgusting, on the contrary, immediately wakes the will — the body says a sharp “no,” and calm contemplation becomes impossible. That's why disgust is so hard to “think your way out of”: it happens before reasoning does. From this point of view, there's no need to be ashamed of it — it's a protective reaction of the will, looking out for you. If the disgust is directed at yourself, Schopenhauer would remind you that the will living in you is the same as in all beings. There is no special vileness in you: there is human nature, equally imperfect in everyone.
disgust.practice: Step back from whatever disgusts you and take a few slow out-breaths. Then name what exactly your “no” is protecting right now.

revenge.text: The desire for revenge usually means you've been caused real pain. Schopenhauer drew an important distinction. Punishment, he wrote, looks to the future: its purpose is to protect, to prevent new harm. Revenge looks to the past, and the past cannot be changed. So revenge, in his view, cannot give what is expected of it: what was done will not be undone, and new pain only multiplies the suffering in a world already overflowing with it. Schopenhauer added a deeper thought: the one who causes pain and the one who suffers are manifestations of one and the same will, so in wounding another the will wounds itself. From this point of view, the force now boiling inside can be turned toward the future: how to protect yourself and keep this from happening again.
revenge.practice: Write: “To keep this from happening again, I need to…” Let the answer contain only steps that protect you and harm no one.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at loved ones is one of the most painful feelings: you love the person and still lash out. Schopenhauer would explain it this way: the will — our constant striving — is invested most heavily precisely in those close to us. From them we want the most: understanding, care, for them to be different. Where desire is stronger, the collision with reality hurts more. Schopenhauer considered a person's character almost unchangeable, and in the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he advised accepting people as they are rather than being angry with them for their nature. From this point of view, anger often flares up in the place of an expectation that “they should be different.” There's no need to be ashamed of it. But it's worth noticing which expectation has just collided with who the person really is.
anger_at_loved.practice: Finish the sentence: “I'm angry because I expect them to be…” Ask yourself: how well does this expectation match who this person is?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone close to you and being unable to stand them at the same time is not a sign of a bad relationship but an almost inevitable side of one. Schopenhauer told of this in his famous parable of the porcupines in Parerga and Paralipomena. On a cold winter's day the porcupines huddle together for warmth, but prick each other with their quills and move apart. The cold drives them together again, the quills wound again, and so they are tossed back and forth until they find a moderate distance at which they can both keep warm and not prick each other too much. From this point of view, your mixed feelings are a natural consequence of closeness: the closer people are, the stronger both the warmth and the pricks. You don't have to choose which feeling is the “real” one. You can look for your own distance — the one at which there is more warmth than pain.
ambivalence.practice: Think: at which moments near this person do you feel warmer, and at which does it prick? What distance would suit you today?

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or even the death of a seriously ill loved one often frightens people: how can you feel this alongside grief? Schopenhauer helps you understand why it's natural. He believed we feel suffering directly and sharply, while satisfaction is felt only as the ending of pain. Relief is exactly such an ending: long strain, fear, sleepless nights finally let go. It is not joy at the loss but a body and soul breathing out for the first time in a long while. And if your loved one suffered greatly, relief can also be a form of compassion — what Schopenhauer considered the basis of love: you felt their pain as your own, and now it has ended. From this point of view, relief and love do not contradict each other.
guilty_relief.practice: Allow yourself one slow out-breath and tell yourself: “It was very hard for me.” There's nothing more you need to prove.

indifference.text: When an event “should” move you but inside it's empty, it's easy to suspect yourself of callousness. Schopenhauer called compassion “the great mystery of ethics.” What's surprising is not that we are sometimes indifferent but that another's pain can become ours at all. Usually, in his view, we live under the “veil of Maya” — we see the world divided into separate beings, where the other is simply “not me.” Compassion happens when this veil becomes transparent for a moment. From this point of view, you can't order yourself to feel compassion, and the absence of feeling is not a verdict. It may mean tiredness, being overloaded with your own pain, or that the event hasn't yet become real to you. Compassion can't be forced, but you can leave room for it — for example, by imagining not the event in general but one particular person.
indifference.practice: Instead of thinking about the event as a whole, picture one particular person within it. Notice whether anything has changed inside — even slightly.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — your job, your city, your role — is strong and understandable. Schopenhauer knew it firsthand: his father was preparing him for a career in commerce, and for several years the young man toiled away in a counting-house until he resolved to leave for study and philosophy. But he also warned that when we change places, we take ourselves along. The will — our restless striving — travels with us to any city. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he wrote that what matters most for happiness is what a person is in themselves, not what they have or how they look in others' eyes. From this point of view, you can hear the urge to escape as a question: what am I myself missing — an occupation, quiet, meaning? Sometimes a change of circumstances is needed, sometimes a change within.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: “There, where I want to escape to, I'll finally be able to…” Does this wish have a small form that's possible already, here?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or “wrong” often takes you by surprise: you decided nothing of the sort, yet the feeling is already there. Schopenhauer described this as the will's main characteristic. In the second volume of The World as Will and Representation he compared the relationship between will and intellect to a strong blind man carrying on his shoulders a lame man who can see. The will wants first; the intellect learns of its desires afterwards and is often surprised by them itself. From this point of view, an attraction that's “not allowed” is neither a decision nor evidence of your depravity, but a movement of the will that your consciousness has simply received news of. Schopenhauer urged neither submitting to the will nor being ashamed of it. He proposed understanding and contemplating. You can calmly look at this desire: what is it seeking, which lack is it answering?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Describe the attraction as if observing it from outside: “The will in me reaches toward… because it lacks…” Just look at what comes out.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of being judged is familiar to many, and it makes simple encounters exhausting. Schopenhauer devoted part of the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life to this. He distinguished three sources of our well-being: what a person is, what they have, and how they appear in others' eyes. And he held that people greatly overrate the third — others' opinion. As he observed, a huge share of our anxieties concerns what others will think, although their thoughts about us are usually fleeting: everyone is busy with their own will and their own worries. From this point of view, your nervousness is understandable, but its object is much smaller than it seems. Schopenhauer advised gradually shifting the weight from others' gaze to what you yourself are. This doesn't require courage all at once — only a habit of noticing.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, ask yourself: what do I value in myself regardless of how this conversation goes? Write down one quality.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: the will, our constant striving, wants to know how everything will turn out. Schopenhauer stressed that future and past exist only in our concepts, while what is truly given is only the present: the one form in which life appears to us at all. Yet we constantly live where we are not — in an imagined “later.” In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life he offered the rule “limitation makes for happiness”: the narrower the circle of our concerns, the fewer reasons for anxiety. From this point of view, you needn't try to take in all possible outcomes at once; you can narrow your gaze to what is happening today and what can be done now. The uncertainty won't disappear, but it will stop filling all of your time.
uncertainty.practice: Draw a small circle and write inside it only what depends on you in the next twenty-four hours. Leave everything else outside the circle.

waiting.text: Waiting makes time drag: everything inside is straining toward one moment that just won't come. For Schopenhauer this is an almost pure picture of the will — a striving that reaches forward and cannot settle. But he also knew a state in which this pull lets go for a while. When we give ourselves entirely to contemplation — of a cloud, a melody, a painting — we stop being only a wanting creature and become simply a looking one. Schopenhauer described this as a “Sabbath” — a day of rest from the penal servitude of the will. From this point of view, waiting needn't be overcome by force. For a few minutes you can switch from “when will it happen” to “what do I see or hear right now.” The waiting will remain, but you'll have little islands of respite.
waiting.practice: Choose one thing near you — a sound, a light, an object — and for two minutes simply take it in, expecting nothing.

quote.text: We keep the Sabbath of the penal servitude of willing; the wheel of Ixion stands still.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: The World as Will and Representation, Vol. 1, § 38 (1819)

regret.text: Regret over something done or left undone knows how to come back again and again: “if only I had…” In his essay “On the Freedom of the Will,” Schopenhauer offered an idea that can unexpectedly lighten this burden. We really do what we want, but what exactly we want follows from our character and the circumstances of that moment. From this point of view, your choice back then was an expression of who you were and what you knew then, not random foolishness. Schopenhauer also spoke of “acquired character” — the knowledge of ourselves we accumulate through experience, including through mistakes. Regret then becomes part of that knowledge: it tells you what truly matters to you rather than proving that you're bad.
regret.practice: Finish the sentence: “This regret taught me that what matters to me is…” Reread it as knowledge about yourself, not as a reproach.

quote.text: Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
quote.source: On the Freedom of the Will (1839)

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is when their absence feels almost like a presence. Schopenhauer understood this double feeling. On the one hand, the will won't let go: it wants precisely this person, and no one else will do. On the other, he wrote about the magic that memory casts over the past and the distant. When we remember, we see the image without the bustle of desires and anxieties that accompanied reality, and so it shines especially brightly. From this point of view, your longing is made of two threads: a real lack, and this soft light of memory. The first you can simply acknowledge — it speaks of the depth of the bond. The second you can cherish: there is something of contemplation in it, in which pain briefly becomes beauty.
longing.practice: Recall one scene with this person and describe it in three or four details — a colour, a sound, a gesture. Stay with this picture.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — news of war, injustice, other people's grief — can become unbearable. Schopenhauer was perhaps the most honest philosopher of suffering: he didn't deny that there is an enormous amount of it in the world. But he considered the main answer to it to be compassion — the ability to feel another's pain as your own. He saw this not as weakness but as the foundation of all morality. From this point of view, your pain for the world is the very best thing Schopenhauer found in human beings. Yet he also knew the danger of drowning. That is why, alongside compassion, he placed art and contemplation — minutes when the will falls silent and you can recover your strength. Protecting such minutes is not an escape from the world but a condition for your fellow-feeling not to run dry.
world_pain.practice: Do one small thing out of compassion — for someone near you or for people far away. Then give yourself five minutes of music or silence.

quote.text: Boundless compassion for all living beings is the firmest and surest guarantee of pure moral conduct.
quote.author: Arthur Schopenhauer

rejection.text: Rejection wounds, and the pain of it is natural: the will in each of us wants to be accepted. Schopenhauer, however, helps us look at it from another side. He believed that each person's choice flows from their own character and their own will — and that will can't be argued with. When you are rejected, what decides is someone else's make-up, their inclinations and lacks, which you didn't choose and can't change. This doesn't always say anything about your worth. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life Schopenhauer insisted that what matters most is what a person is in themselves, not how others rate them. From this point of view, a refusal is an event that hurts to live through, but not a verdict on who you are.
rejection.practice: Write down three qualities you have regardless of who does or doesn't choose you.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very old and very deep, and nobody makes it up. Schopenhauer knew ruptures firsthand: after a bitter quarrel with his mother he didn't see her for many years. His philosophy explains why this fear is so strong: the will clings to what is dear to it and senses loss long before it happens. Schopenhauer advised cultivating what he called inner wealth — interests, thoughts, the ability to find support in yourself. This doesn't mean giving up closeness or loving less. Rather, it means that if you lean not only on another person, the fear of loss stops being a matter of survival. From this point of view, inner wealth is not a wall but a floor under your feet.
abandonment.practice: Name one activity or interest that fills you even when you're alone. Give it at least ten minutes today.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love can feel like a pain out of proportion to anything else. In “The Metaphysics of Sexual Love,” Schopenhauer explained why. He believed that in intense love it is not only the individual who speaks but something much greater — the will to live itself, which he called “the genius of the species.” That's why passion feels like destiny, and its failure like a catastrophe: something ancient and immense is striving through one person. From this point of view, the depth of your pain is neither exaggeration nor weakness of character; this is how a force greater than any of us works. Schopenhauer promised no quick consolation, but he pointed to a respite — art, music, contemplation. In them the pain doesn't vanish, but for a while it stops being only yours and becomes something all humans share.
unrequited.practice: Find a song or poem about unrequited love. Listen to it or read it, noticing: a great many people before you have suffered over this.

humiliation.text: Humiliation wounds deeply because it strikes at your dignity. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer took apart what people call honour. He scathingly mocked the “knightly” code by which an insulted person supposedly becomes covered in disgrace until they take revenge. Schopenhauer considered this absurd: rudeness and insult speak of the one who commits them, not of the one they strike. A person's true worth, in his view, lies in what they are, not in others' opinion, which may be foolish, malicious or hasty. From this point of view: you were hurt, and that deserves to be acknowledged, but your dignity does not pass into the hands of the one who tried to take it away.
humiliation.practice: Finish the sentence: “What this act says about them is…” And then: “About me, it says only that I was hurt.”

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can accompany a person for years, and almost always there are other people's gazes and comparisons behind it. Schopenhauer offered an unusual view of the body. For him the body is not an object we carry around but our will made visible: the way life in us shows itself outwardly. We know our body in two ways — from the inside, as feeling, movement and desire, and from the outside, as an image among other images. Shame lives almost entirely in the second way — in the view from outside, often someone else's. From this point of view, you can return to the first: your body is what you live with, breathe with, feel with, not a picture to be graded. Schopenhauer in general advised against giving others' opinions power over what you are.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes for a minute and feel your body from the inside: your breath, warmth, support. Notice how it feels without a mirror.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, a sense of injustice and loneliness is added to the pain. Schopenhauer was one of the few philosophers who didn't try to prettify suffering. He considered it the basic fabric of life, not a punishment, a mistake or a personal failure. From this point of view, illness is not a sign that you did something wrong: it is part of the common human lot, shared by countless beings. Schopenhauer valued health highly and understood how much it means — so he would never say illness is “for the best.” But he knew that even on hard days there can be minutes when the will falls quiet: music, the view from a window, quiet contemplation. They don't heal, but they offer a respite, and you can allow yourself that.
illness.practice: For a couple of minutes, find something pleasant to look at or listen to. Allow yourself simply to take it in, without thinking about the illness.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a good and well-earned feeling. In the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, Schopenhauer drew a distinction that helps you enjoy it without needless doubts. Pride, he wrote, is an inner conviction of one's own worth in some respect, while vanity is the desire to awaken such a conviction in others. Pride is calm and needs no audience; vanity is noisy and depends on others' approval. From this point of view, pride in work well done is one of those goods that lie within yourself — and these Schopenhauer ranked above all others. There's no need to be ashamed of it, nor to prove it to anyone. You can simply know: I did this, and I did it well.
pride.practice: Say to yourself, silently, with no witnesses: “I did this.” Notice what it feels like to have pride that needs no one's confirmation.

melancholy.text: Gentle melancholy is a state in which sadness is somehow good. Schopenhauer understood this like no one else. He believed that music expresses not this or that particular sorrow but sorrow itself, its essence — and so, listening to a sad melody, we live through it as if without our own pain. Melancholy is similar: the sadness is there, but it doesn't demand or grasp; it contemplates. From this point of view, melancholy is a rare case in which the will falls quiet but the feeling remains. Schopenhauer, following Aristotle, noted that deep, creative natures are prone to melancholy. That doesn't mean it's required. But if it has come, there's no need to hurry it away — you can stay in it and see the world a little more clearly.
melancholy.practice: Put on music in tune with your mood and listen without doing anything else. Notice how the sadness in it grows softer.
